extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of philosophy/history of science; readers of Bacon's Novum Organum
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and signs (per Bacon and commentator) for judging whether a body of learning qualifies as a genuine science: signs of growth, origin, consensus, aims, and institutional/psychological causes of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth and progress (signa ex incrementis et progressibus)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Capienda etiam sunt signa ex incrementis et progressibus philosopharum et scientiarum.’ Doctrines founded in nature grow and are augmented; those founded in opinion merely vary and do not increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine science exhibits cumulative increase over time — new discoveries, applications, and refinements. If a field shows only variations of opinion without cumulative augmentations, either it is not susceptible to scientific treatment or a scientific method has yet to be discovered. Example/contrast: mechanical arts steadily grow by experiment and practice; purely dogmatic systems do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable practical fruits and applications (fructus/operativa pars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences should produce useful works and operations (arts, inventions, medicines, mechanical arts) — the presence of operative, practical fruits is a sign of healthy science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concrete applications, technical improvements, and operational advances as evidence of a science’s vitality. Bacon stresses that astronomy, optics, medicine, mechanics, and even moral/civil philosophy gain from being tied to natural philosophy; absence of practical fruits signals stagnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founded in nature (not merely opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those doctrines 'in natura fundata sunt' (founded in nature) grow; doctrines grounded in mere opinion do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a field builds from observations and nature (facts) toward generalisations, rather than from authoritative assertions or abstract dogma. Preference for empirically grounded inquiry over rhetorical or purely speculative argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' confession of ignorance or limits (propria confessio authorum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign of sound science is when its practitioners/ authors, on reconsideration, acknowledge nature’s subtilty, obscurities, and the limits of human understanding — provoking further inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive sign: openness about what is unknown and willingness to be led back to investigation. Anti-pattern: authors who, through pride or envy, declare things impossible or place limits on inquiry, thereby discouraging others and turning failure onto nature itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence (or presence) of enforced consensus and genuine disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread dissension and multiplicity of schools indicate that the path from sense to intellect was not well secured; conversely, 'verus consensus' (true consensus) is a sign but must satisfy conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess consensuses critically: true consensus requires competent judges, thorough prior examination of the matter, and freedom from mutual influence. Large numbers consenting from prejudice or authority (sequacitas et coitio) are not reliable signs of truth. Persistent controversies about core principles indicate a lack of sound demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct origin/rooting of a science (radices / materia originaria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences separated from their roots in natural philosophy fail to grow; the sciences ought to be branches nourished by a general Natural Philosophy (the 'mater' or 'trunk').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a particular science remains connected to broader empirical and conceptual foundations (laws of nature, motions, textures, affects, intellectual prehensions). Disciplines isolated from these roots tend toward superficiality and variety without depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper curricular aim / teleology of science (meta scientiarum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true and legitimate end (meta) of the sciences is to endow human life with new works, discoveries, and powers ('ut dotetur vita humana novis inventis et copiis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific programme or curriculum should be judged by whether it is oriented toward augmenting human capabilities and delivering useful, concrete benefits. If the aim is merely intellectual satisfaction, reputation, profit, or controversy, progress toward genuine augmentation will be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between knowledge for its own sake and utility (veritas vs utilitas)
rubrics_metrics.description: While Bacon acknowledges the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake and the intellectual pleasures of learning, he repeatedly insists sciences should be conjoined with action and usefulness ('Appetunt enim homines...'), and warns against a doctrine whose end is only satisfaction or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether inquiry privileges illuminating, explanatory experiments (lucifera experimenta) and fruitful, usable results; beware both excessive utilitarian narrowness and purely self-regarding scholarship that avoids rigorous truth-seeking. The commentator notes tension between pure contemplation and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and motivational causes of stagnation (ambitus, meritoria/professorial motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dominant cause of limited scientific progress is scholars’ vocational motives: many pursue knowledge for teaching, profit, reputation, or contention rather than for enlargement of the mass of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine institutional incentives: if university/professional structures reward narrow teaching, lucrum or fame, or convert knowledge to immediate gains, this will reduce incentives for genuine discovery. Positive sign: inventive, glory-seeking artisans sometimes advance practice when they invest labor and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical interruption and limited productive epochs (tempora / sacculorum numerus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long historical gaps, the limited number of prolific centuries, and destructive historical events (inundations, barbarian incursions) are causes that explain slow accumulations of science across ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a science historically, account for loss of memory, discontinuities, and periods when natural philosophy was neglected. The commentator accepts Bacon's tripartite historical scheme (Greek, Roman, modern) as explaining scarcity of continuous growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive specialization without return to general survey (particulares non reductae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular sciences, once constituted and separated, cease to be nourished by the general Natural Philosophy unless they are cyclically returned and reconnected; without this, they remain superficial and merely varied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy development requires a cycle: natural philosophy produces particular sciences, and those particular sciences must be fed back into and re-examined by natural philosophy. Evaluate whether disciplinary specialisation includes mechanisms for reintegration and foundational renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-scientific dogmas and pronouncements of impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When practitioners declare certain true forms or differences impossible of discovery (e.g., 'formae inventu impossibiles'), this is a sign of intellectual failing — arrogance that converts authors' weakness into aspersions on nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat categorical claims of impossibility skeptically; they often reflect the limits, pride, or envy of authors rather than a provable barrier in nature. Favor humility and methodological openness that leave room for further investigation.
